fields.meta_title: Password Reset Form Builder for IT Teams | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build a password reset form that names the locked account, sends each request to IT, and never asks for a password. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build a Password Reset Form That Never Asks for a Password
fields.hero_description: Build a password reset form that sends each lockout to IT with the account named and no password typed in.
fields.features_heading: What IT Needs Before It Resets Anything
fields.features_subheading: Describe who gets locked out and which accounts they use. Emergent builds the form, the queue IT works from, and the alerts.
fields.feature_1:
No field for the old or new password

The form asks for a name, work email, employee ID, the locked account, and what happened. No password passes through it, and none ever sits in the request table IT reads.
fields.feature_2:
Requests that go to the account's owner

Pick Email and the request lands in the help desk queue. Pick Payroll and it goes to whoever runs payroll access, with the employee ID and work email already filled in.
fields.feature_3:
A callback before anyone resets it

The request record carries a Verified box the tech ticks after calling the number on file. The app will not mark a reset done until that box holds a check and the tech's name.
fields.feature_4:
Urgent when the account may be misused

Answer that another person may have signed in, and the request is marked Urgent. The security lead gets a Slack message naming the account and the time it was filed.
fields.feature_5:
Repeat lockouts, counted per person

A dashboard counts requests by account and by month. Anyone with 3 or more resets in 30 days lands on a short list, with the date of each reset and the account it was for.
fields.feature_6:
Your GitHub repository holds the code

On paid plans, export the full codebase to your GitHub repository and run the form beside your current help desk. The request table and the routing rules move with it.
fields.why_title: Why Build Password Reset Forms With Emergent?
fields.why_description: A reset request sent by email asks IT to trust whoever wrote it. The form Emergent builds adds a callback to the number on file.

fields.usecase_heading: Who Is Locked Out, and Who Resets It
fields.tab_content_1:
Back into email 14 minutes after the lockout

Ferelith Ainscough at Kittiwake Accounting is locked out of email at 8:52 am. She files from her phone with her employee ID and "Forgot password." Tech Cosmo Lightbody calls her desk extension from the staff directory, not a number typed into the form. He resets the account at 9:06 am.
fields.tab_content_2:
If someone else used it, the security lead hears first

Leasing agent Peregrine Gorringe at Lowestoft Residential sees a payroll sign-in he never made. He picks Payroll and "Someone else may have used it" on the form. That answer marks the request Urgent and sends security lead Ondine Cobbold a Slack message. It stays at the top of the help desk queue until she closes it.
fields.tab_content_3:
A 2:10 am lockout waits on Kwabena first

Night shift at Tumbridge Cold Storage runs from 10 pm to 6 am. Philippa Lusk is locked out of her scanner sign-in at 2:10 am and files from the break-room kiosk. Requests filed in those hours go to shift supervisor Kwabena Hesketh, who confirms she is on shift. On-call tech Dashiell Brannagh then gets it by email.
fields.tab_content_4:
Who keeps getting locked out, by name and count

Fenmarch Hotels runs one IT team for 3 properties. Its October dashboard shows 58 reset requests: 23 for email, 19 for the front desk, 10 for payroll, and 6 for bookings. Four staff filed 14 of them, each with 3 or more in 30 days. IT director Yevgenia Tolliver books the four a self-service setup session.

plan.angle: Results for this query are login-screen tutorials and end-user help articles on recovering one account. This page treats the password reset form as the request a locked-out employee sends to IT: five fields (name, work email, employee ID, the account, what happened), no field for any password, a callback to the number on file before the reset, an urgent path when someone else may have used the account, a supervisor check on night shifts and a monthly count of resets by account. General IT tickets, access grants and device requests belong to sibling pages, which the FAQ links instead of answering. No security certification claims; the NIST lines are quoted inside their own scope.
